newsitem.title: USA: Minn. Twins say pessimistic about future in state.
newsitem.headline: Minn. Twins say pessimistic about future in state.

text.p: Minnesota Twins owner Carl Pohlad has told lawmakers their failure to approve financing for a new stadium in the last legislative session has made him "extremely pessimistic" about the future of major league baseball in the state.
As a result of "legislative indifference," the Twins will explore other options, Pohlad wrote in a letter to legislative leaders Tuesday.

"We have invested a great deal of effort to keep major league baseball in Minnesota as have many legislators, particularly the bill's authors," Pohlad wrote. "We do not intend to continue the effort unless and until we are convinced that there is a leadership commitment to resolve this matter before we must face the decision to terminate our lease."

Minnesota lawmakers rejected numerous financing plans for a new $400 million retractable-roof ballpark for the Twins during the session concluded Monday. None of the proposals made it to the full house or senate for consideration.

The team's lease at the Metrodome runs through 2011, but includes an escape clause that would allow the team to leave after the 1998 season if ticket sales are poor compared to the rest of the American League or the ballclub loses money three years in a row.
The Twins reported losses each of the past two seasons.
Minnesota Gov. Arne Carlson, a stadium supporter, urged a full legislative vote on the financing at the time, saying that the failure to reach a plan could jeopardize the team's future.
Pohlad's letter came as no surprise to the governor, spokesman Brian Dietz said Thursday.
Carlson has called for a special session to discuss education funding plans, a minimum wage increase and raises for state employees, lawmakers and judges, Dietz said.

Financing for arenas and stadiums could be part of the special session only if legislative leaders agree to discuss them and at this point they are not in favor of adding them to the agenda, Dietz said.
Carlson and legislative leaders have scheduled a meeting for Tuesday to discuss the scope of the special session and set a date to begin negotiations.
